guidance.cx-action-area:
Use action area when a complete content block needs contextual actions without changing the block's normal layout. It wraps any content that should own local actions, such as a summary card, labeled details, a status block, or a compact signal.

Use info, askAi, support, and editable for the standard block actions. They render as one right-aligned action group in this order: Info, Ask AI, Support, custom actions, Edit. Use actions only for extra custom actions that belong to the same block.

The outline and action group reveal after a short delay so passing over content does not feel twitchy. The action group should stay on one line. When it no longer fits, it first hides shortcut hints from every button. If it still does not fit, buttons with icons become icon-only buttons and expose the original action text in a tooltip. Keep actions local to the wrapped content. Do not use action area as a page toolbar, a card replacement, or a way to hide primary actions. Shortcuts should only trigger while the area is hovered or focused, and each visible shortcut must actually work in that context.
guidance.cx-alert:
Use alerts for contextual feedback that explains a state the user needs to notice and understand. Do not default to alerts: if the message has no urgency and does not need extra attention, use normal body text instead. Alerts are not for ordinary descriptive copy. Use mood to describe the message, from light emphasis to stronger intervention: default when information only needs to stand out a little more than body text, info when informational context is more important to see, success for confirmation, warning for preventable risk, and danger for failure or a blocked action.

Alerts should be short, actionable, and calm. They are not banners, toasts, or field validation. They sit on the canvas, close to the thing they explain. Add a canonical button action only when the next useful step can happen directly from the alert. Set its real mood or transparency when the default quiet button is not right; loading and disabled behavior stay with the button. Make an alert dismissible only when the user can safely ignore it after reading.
guidance.cx-badge:
Use badges as compact attention markers. The default badge should usually appear without a count: it says there is something worth noticing, not how much work is waiting. This is the normal choice for filters, controls, navigation items, or places where the user only needs a small visual signal.

Add a count only when the number itself helps the user act, such as unread notifications, events, selected items, or active filters. Do not add a number just because the component supports one. Most badges should stay without a count.
guidance.cx-banner:
Use banners for rare, important, time-sensitive information that needs broad attention at the top of the affected surface. Use quieter inline or page-level feedback when the message does not earn that interruption.

A banner must not cover essential navigation, actions, or page content. Dismissibility controls whether a transient message can be removed; it does not decide whether the layout becomes obstructed. Let users dismiss transient banners. A persistent unresolved state may remain visible, but it needs a direct action, acknowledgement, or clear explanation of why it cannot disappear.

Keep banner copy short, direct, and specific. Include an action only when it is the real next step.
guidance.cx-avatar:
Use avatars to identify a person, account, team, or system at a glance. Prefer an image when it is stable and recognizable. Otherwise, use the name so the initials stay consistent and readable.

Avatars should support recognition, not decoration. Keep the color automatic unless the surrounding product already has a meaningful color choice. Use the badge only as a small attention marker, and let it keep the default badge color so identity and status do not compete.
guidance.cx-breadcrumbs:
Use breadcrumbs when the user is inside a real hierarchy and needs to understand where the current page lives. They are not a replacement for back, and they should not appear on shallow pages just to fill space.

Keep the first and current level visible. When the path is too deep or the space is too narrow, collapse the middle levels into the hidden-level menu. Use switchable crumbs only when the user can stay in the same kind of view while changing a scope, source, customer, or other level in the hierarchy.
guidance.cx-budget:
Use budgets to show how a value relates to a known limit. They work best when the user needs to understand pace, remaining capacity, or whether usage is getting close to a boundary. Use percent when the exact unit is not important, currency when the amount itself changes the decision, and unit for things like seats, credits, hours, or storage. Use unitLabel for the text shown after counted values, such as seats, credits, hours, or GB.

Use the compact variant when the budget is a small supporting signal. Use the detailed variant when both the current value and the total need to be visible. Favor describes what good looks like: low when a smaller value is better, high when a larger value is better. Add a hint only when the extra context helps the user act, such as expiry, renewal, or reserved budget.
guidance.cx-button:
Use the default button for almost every action. When in doubt, use default. Primary is only for the action that moves the user toward their goal, and it should usually appear once per view or once inside the element it belongs to.

Use danger for destructive actions, and make the surrounding flow add enough friction before something is lost. Use transparent when the action should stay quiet inside dense UI, toolbars, menus, or supporting controls. Use rounded only when a pill shape is intentional. Button text should name the action, not the state: "Delete file" beats "Confirm". Use shortcutParts only to display a shortcut that is handled by the surrounding context; the button itself does not own keyboard shortcut behavior. Icon-only buttons need a clear ariaLabel.
guidance.cx-card:
Use cards to group one self-contained piece of content. The default card uses a 4px surface-alt frame, with the header sitting directly on that frame and the content inside a rounded surface island.

Add border when a repeated card needs a clearer object edge, such as dense boards; bordered cards use the 1px line instead of the 4px frame. Add shadow when the card needs a little lift from the canvas without changing its structure. Add a header when the card needs a title, icon, status, local menu, or meta content. Use the meta slot for small supporting status such as a tag. Use menuItems only for actions that belong to that card. Set interactive only when the whole card is a real target, such as opening a detail view. Use padding="none" only when the content needs to sit flush, such as tables, charts, media, or custom layouts. Use padding="large" when a card needs a roomier 16px rhythm inside the header and content island.
guidance.cx-code-field:
Use code fields only for short one-time verification codes. They are for moments where the user is copying a six-character code from email, SMS, an authenticator app, or a recovery flow.

Do not use a code field for passwords, serial numbers, IDs, invite codes, API keys, or long tokens. Passwords need password fields. Other long values need normal text fields because the user may need to read, select, edit, or paste the value as one piece. Keep validation close to the field, and let paste work generously.
guidance.cx-split-button:
Use split buttons only when one action has a clear default and the menu contains close variations of that same action. The main side runs the default action; the chevron opens related alternatives.

Do not use a split button for unrelated actions or as a way to hide decisions the user must make first. If there is no obvious default action, use a menu button instead. Keep labels direct, keep destructive alternatives visibly dangerous, and use primary only when the default action is the main path forward.
guidance.cx-variant:
Use variants to show realistic examples of how a component can be used. Each tab should represent a meaningful scenario, state, or composition that helps someone understand the component in context, not just a prop value in isolation.

Variants are not a full workbench and should not try to expose every prop. Use them when the useful question is "what does this look like in real product use?" Keep the names short, choose examples people would actually build, and let the specimen do the explaining.
guidance.cx-big-checkbox:
Use a big checkbox when one binary choice needs more room than a small checkbox can give it. It works well for permissions, setup choices, and options where the label needs a short explanation.

The state is only selected or not selected. The optional icon sits on the far right as a 24px square-subtle icon. Use iconMood only to color that icon treatment; it should not change the checkbox surface. Use the content slot below the text for small supporting content that belongs inside the option, such as metadata or a compact preview. Keep the copy short and make the whole item easy to scan. If the choice is part of a long form or a dense table, use a regular checkbox instead.
guidance.cx-big-radio:
Use a big radio when the user must choose one clear option from a small set. It is best for choices that need a title, a short explanation, or a more touch-friendly target.

The optional icon sits on the far right as a 24px square-subtle icon. Use iconMood only to color that icon treatment; it should not change the radio surface. Use the content slot below the text for small supporting content that belongs inside the option, such as metadata or a compact progress signal. Keep the options parallel so they are easy to compare. If the choice is simple and space is tight, use regular radios instead.
guidance.cx-button-group:
Use a button group for a small set of closely related choices where one choice is active at a time. It should feel faster than a dropdown and clearer than several separate buttons.

Keep labels short and make each option the same kind of decision. Disabled choices are skipped by the tab stop and every navigation key; never leave focus trapped on an unavailable choice. If there are many options or the labels become long, use a dropdown instead.
guidance.cx-calendar:
Use a calendar when the date itself matters in relation to nearby days. It is useful for planning, scheduling, and choosing dates where weekday context helps. Date picker and date span picker use the same calendar so month navigation, constraints, focus, and selection stay consistent.

Use single selection for one date and range selection for a start and end date. Use embedded only inside another floating surface. Do not use a calendar when the user only needs to enter a known date quickly. In that case, a date field is quieter and faster.
guidance.cx-chart:
Use charts to show shape, trend, comparison, or proportion. A chart should answer a real question faster than a table would.

Keep the chart focused. If the user needs exact values, pair it with a table or use a simpler metric instead.
guidance.cx-checkbox:
Use a checkbox for an independent on/off choice. It should describe a state that can be true or false without changing the meaning of nearby controls.

Write the label as the thing being enabled. Avoid negative labels, because they make checked and unchecked states harder to reason about.
guidance.cx-code-block:
Use a code block when the user needs to read or copy code, commands, logs, or structured text. It should preserve spacing and make the content feel separate from body copy.

Keep surrounding explanation short. If the code is only a tiny value, use inline code or a snippet instead.
guidance.cx-color-picker:
Use a color picker when choosing a raw palette hue is the actual task. It is useful for labels, charts, and visual customization where the color itself is the choice.

Do not use semantic moods such as success, warning, danger, primary, or accent as selectable colors. Those belong in mood props. Keep free color choice rare in product UI.
guidance.cx-context-dialog:
Use a context dialog for a small decision that belongs to the thing the user just interacted with. It should feel local, quick, and specific.

Do not use it for heavy workflows or important confirmations. If the decision affects the whole page or needs more space, use a dialog.
guidance.cx-date-picker:
Use a date picker when the user needs one specific date. It should make choosing a nearby date easy while still allowing direct entry when the date is known.

Keep helper text close to the field only when it prevents mistakes. Do not add extra explanation for obvious dates. If empty, the picker placeholder should read like Select date unless a selected value is already present.
guidance.cx-date-span-picker:
Use a date span picker when the user needs a start and end date that belong together. It is best for reports, filters, bookings, and time windows.

Make the selected range easy to understand at a glance. If the range has limits or consequences, say that before the user commits. If empty, the picker placeholder should read like Select date range unless a selected value is already present.
guidance.cx-dialog:
Use a dialog when the user must make a focused decision without losing the current page. It should be reserved for important choices, short forms, or confirmations that need attention. Confirm dialogs map Escape to Cancel and Mod+Enter to the primary action; info dialogs map Mod+Enter to Close. Their shortcut hints sit outside the buttons and appear when the footer is hovered.

Keep the dialog small and purposeful. If the content grows into a workflow, it probably belongs on its own page or in a fullscreen dialog. Outside clicks should not dismiss a dialog by default. Enable dismissOnClickOutside only for low-consequence dialogs where accidental closure cannot lose work. Supply menuItems only when the dialog needs secondary actions that belong to its current task; an empty or omitted collection leaves the header menu out.
guidance.cx-detail-panel:
Use a detail panel to inspect or edit one object without losing the surrounding collection. Set placement to container when the panel belongs to a positioned workspace and viewport when it must cover the full application height. The panel owns its positioning and responsive behavior; consumers set width or minWidth and arrange the content inside it, never recreate the drawer with page-level fixed positioning.

Keep child overlays layered. A menu, picker, popover, or dialog opened from the panel closes before the panel responds to Escape or outside interaction. Enable dismissOnClickOutside only when losing the panel is safe. Do not guard dismissal with selectors.
guidance.cx-divider:
Use a divider to separate groups that need a visible pause. It should help the eye understand structure, not decorate the page.

If spacing alone is enough, skip the divider. Too many lines make an interface feel heavier than it is.
guidance.cx-validation-message:
Use a validation message to explain state or recovery near the field or action it belongs to. Preserve its meaning in every presentation: status stays neutral, info stays informational, success confirms, warning warns, and error blocks or fails. Global presentation must not turn them all into danger.

Write it in plain language. Do not blame the user, and do not show validation before the user has had a fair chance to act.
guidance.cx-expansion-panel:
Use an expansion panel for secondary information that is useful but not always needed. It helps keep the page calm while still making details easy to reach.

The heading must clearly promise what will open. Avoid hiding critical information inside a collapsed panel.
guidance.cx-file-upload:
Use file upload when the user is adding a file as part of a task. The control should make accepted file types, limits, and current file state easy to understand.

Use the button variant inline in a form when the file is one field among others. Use the zone variant when uploading is the primary action of the surface and the extra room to drag, browse, and preview a list of files earns its place. Both variants accept the same accept, maxSize, and multiple limits, and both surface a rejected file with a specific reason.

Keep one selected-files model from input through output: always pass and read the files array. Single mode limits it to zero or one item; multiple mode may contain several. Do not maintain separate file, hasFile, or fileName state. Show the selected files, upload progress, or the next required action.
guidance.cx-item-card:
Use an item card for a row that pairs a labelled thing with one action, such as a settings toggle, a connected device, or a linked account. The icon and heading identify the item; the trailing slot holds a single control.

Keep the trailing control to one clear action. If a row needs several actions or rich content, use a full card or a detail view instead.
guidance.cx-kpi:
Use a KPI to lead with one number that matters and just enough context to make it meaningful: a trend, a target, or a short comparison. It belongs on dashboards and summaries, not inside dense tables.

Show only the context that changes a decision. Too many trends, bars, and footnotes turn a headline metric back into noise.
guidance.cx-rating:
Use a rating to capture or show a score on a small fixed scale. It is interactive by default; set readonly to display an average, including half values.

Keep the scale small and consistent across the product. If exact precision matters more than a quick impression, a number field or slider may be clearer.
guidance.cx-reaction:
Use a reaction to let someone respond to content with a familiar icon and see how many others did the same. The selected state marks the viewer's own reaction.

Choose an icon whose meaning is immediately recognizable, such as thumbs-up or heart. Keep reactions lightweight and optional. If a response needs words or a real decision, use a comment or a named action instead.
guidance.cx-text-shimmer:
Use a text shimmer for a short label that signals active work — generating, thinking, or streaming. The label stays continuously readable while a narrow highlight travels across it; reduced-motion removes the highlight.

Show it only while something is genuinely happening, and keep the label short. For measurable work, a progress bar tells the user more.
guidance.cx-fullscreen-dialog:
Use a fullscreen dialog when a focused task needs a large temporary canvas but should still read as a dialog, not a route change. It uses the standard dialog overlay behind it, opens with space on the top and sides, and keeps rounded top corners so the app context remains perceptible.

The component is intentionally blank: no heading, description, footer, or action buttons. Put the full experience in the content slot and provide any local navigation, save, or cancel controls inside that slot. Use closeButton only when a close affordance is appropriate; it sits in the overlay's top-right corner outside the canvas.
guidance.cx-grid:
Use a grid when items need to line up in columns and respond cleanly to available space. It is best for cards, metrics, and repeated content blocks.

The grid should serve the content, not force it. If the items need to be read in a strict order, a list may be clearer.
guidance.cx-icon:
Use icons to support recognition, status, or compact actions. An icon should clarify the interface, not replace words when the meaning could be unclear.

Keep icon use consistent. If an icon needs explanation every time, it probably needs text or a tooltip.
guidance.cx-icon-button:
Use an icon button for compact actions where the icon is already familiar or the space is constrained. It is best for repeated tools and secondary actions.

Always make the accessible name specific. Use rounded when the button should read as a circular control, such as floating or overlay chrome. If the action is important or unfamiliar, use a text button instead.
guidance.cx-image:
Use an image when the user benefits from seeing the actual thing. It should support recognition, inspection, or context.

Avoid decorative images in product UI unless they clearly improve comprehension. Empty or broken image states should still feel intentional.
guidance.cx-inline:
Use inline layout for a small row of related items. It keeps actions, labels, and small metadata aligned without creating a new visual block.

Do not use it for content that needs to wrap into paragraphs or compare across rows. When the row gets crowded, move to a stack or grid.
guidance.cx-text-field:
Use a text field for short free text. The label should name the value the user is entering, and the field should stay close to its label.

Do not use placeholders. Put examples, constraints, and format help in hint text. Do not use it for long notes, rich text, or values with strict formats unless the formatting help is clear.
guidance.cx-email-field:
Use an email field when the user is entering an email address. It owns the label, name, accessibility label, native email keyboard, browser autofill, and email-specific format expectation.

Do not use a generic text field for email addresses. Do not configure the browser plumbing locally. Do not use placeholders. Put examples, domain rules, or restrictions in hint text, and show validation directly beneath the field.
guidance.cx-phone-field:
Use a phone field when the user is entering a phone number and country code matters. It owns the label, input names, accessibility labels, autocomplete behavior, and country-code selector so products do not rebuild that pattern locally.

Do not split the country code into a separate nearby dropdown. Do not use it for numeric identifiers. Be forgiving about spaces and local phone-number formatting.
guidance.cx-lightbox:
Use a lightbox when the user needs to inspect media without leaving the current page. It should feel like a temporary closer look.

Keep controls minimal and predictable. If the media needs editing or a complex workflow, use a dedicated view instead.
guidance.cx-list-view:
Use a list view for repeated items that need to be scanned vertically. It is good for navigation, search results, and compact summaries.

Make each row readable without forcing the user to open it. Put the most important information first.
guidance.cx-loader:
Use a loader when content is coming and the wait is short enough that the user should stay in place. It tells the user the system is working.

Prefer skeletons or preserved layout when the shape of the content is known. Do not use loaders to hide slow or unclear states.
guidance.cx-log:
Use a log to show a sequence of system events or process steps. It should help the user understand what happened and what may need attention. Build its one complete log model with CxLog.of(entries); each entry owns its step and any timestamp, description, or author, while the log derives connector positions from the final sequence.

Keep entries short and ordered. If the user needs to act on an entry, make the action easy to find.
guidance.cx-log-step:
Use a log step for one item in a process history. The status, label, and time should quickly explain where the process stands.

Do not overload each step with prose. A log is for scanning first, detail second.
guidance.cx-markdown:
Use markdown rendering for trusted, formatted content that needs simple structure. It is useful for notes, guidance, and generated summaries. Article markdown centres its reading measure on an open canvas; set align to start when the article is embedded beside navigation or another fixed column and needs to share the adjacent content edge.

Keep markdown restrained in product UI. Too many heading levels, links, or styles can make the page feel unmanaged.
guidance.cx-menu:
Use a menu for a short list of contextual actions or compact choices. It should appear where the actions belong, and it must declare whether it is trigger, inline, or context presentation. A trigger presentation uses one real button marked cxMenuTrigger; context presentation opens at the invocation point without activating the object beneath it.

Do not use a menu to hide primary actions. If something is the main next step, keep it visible. Flat items are actions unless type is choice. A group with selection makes its leaf items choices unless an item explicitly declares type action. Actions never acquire choice state or change currentId. Single choices close and update currentId; multiple choices stay open while the owner updates selected state.
guidance.cx-metric:
Use a metric for one important number and its label. It should help the user understand status quickly.

Do not pack too many metrics together. A metric loses power when everything on the page is shouting.
guidance.cx-option:
Use an option for one selectable item inside a choice list. The label should make the choice understandable without extra context.

Use supporting text only when it helps compare options. Keep descriptions close to the label so the row reads as one choice, not two distant columns. Use mood only for semantic signal: danger for destructive actions, success for positive state, warning for caution, info for neutral information, and primary or accent only when the row genuinely needs that emphasis. Use shortcutParts or appendIcon for trailing metadata/actions that truly belong at the far edge. Avoid repeating the same words across every option. Use active for the current navigation target, such as the row reached by arrow keys. Use selected for the committed value. Keep selectedHighlight on when the whole row should read as selected; turn it off when another control, such as a checkbox, already carries the selection state.
guidance.cx-option-group:
Use an option group when related choices need a shared label or small count. It should create structure quietly through spacing and subdued text, not through boxed chrome, dividers, or heavy headings.

Keep groups meaningful. If the grouping does not change how the user decides, it adds friction.
guidance.cx-pagination:
Use pagination when there are more items than should be shown at once and the user benefits from stable pages. It works well for lists that are browsed or revisited.

Do not paginate tiny lists. If the user is likely to search or filter instead, make those controls strong.
guidance.cx-number-field:
Use a number field when the user must enter an exact numeric value. It should make units, limits, and invalid values clear.

Do not use placeholders. Put examples, constraints, units, and ranges in hint text. Use a slider only when approximate adjustment is the main task. Exact values belong in a number field.
guidance.cx-placeholder:
Use a placeholder to reserve space for content that is missing, loading, or not configured yet. It should explain the empty state without feeling broken.

Do not use placeholders as decoration. They should either help the user wait, understand, or act.
guidance.cx-progress-bar:
Use a progress bar when completion has a clear start and end. Give it a visible label or ariaLabel that names what is progressing, and associate any useful hint. A progress indicator is passive information, never a disabled control.

Avoid fake precision. If progress cannot be measured honestly, use indeterminate progress or a loader instead. Reduced motion keeps indeterminate progress still rather than merely slowing an endless sweep.
guidance.cx-qr-code:
Use a QR code when scanning is genuinely faster than typing or copying. It is useful for device pairing, login handoff, and sharing links across devices.

Always provide a fallback. A QR code should never be the only way to complete an important task.
guidance.cx-query-element:
Use a query element to present one readable part of a structured condition. The query field composes grouped field, operator, and value parts into complete clauses.

Keep labels in user language. Consumers should not assemble query logic from visual elements or expose implementation terms to the user.
guidance.cx-query-field:
Use a query field when the user needs to build, inspect, and edit SQL-style conditions in one text-field surface. Supply fields with compatible operators and typed value sources; the component guides field → operator → value, then asks for an explicit AND or OR before another condition. Done appears once the expression can end, and Mod+Enter finishes without opening another connector. In multiple-value lists, Enter toggles the active value; Space does the same while search text is empty. When an unchanged editor is empty, Left and Right move the ink caret across committed query parts while the matching autocomplete follows it. Up and Down move through the current options, Enter applies the active option, and Backspace removes the condition owning the caret; unfinished or dirty edits stay in place so work is never discarded. Persistent per-clause remove buttons are intentionally omitted, while the edit popover keeps a contextual Remove filter action for pointer and touch use.

Keep growVertically on when the full query should remain visible. Set it to false in compact toolbars or dense table headers where one fixed row and horizontal scrolling protect the surrounding layout. Use manual value filtering for remote option sets and keep loading or failure local to that value source. The value is flat: consumers must apply their documented SQL precedence when AND and OR are mixed. Do not use a query field for simple text search, and add parentheses only when grouped logic becomes a real product requirement.
guidance.cx-radio:
Use radios when the user must choose exactly one option from a small set. All options should be visible so the user can compare them.

Avoid using radios for many items or very long labels. A dropdown or searchable control will be easier to scan.
guidance.cx-dropdown:
Use a dropdown for choosing from a larger or less frequently changed set. It keeps the page calm when showing all options would be too much.

Use clear labels and either a selected default or a placeholder shaped as Select [thing], such as Select entity or Select language. Use Select only when no clearer object fits. Required is the default; set optional only when the field is not required. Turn on searchable when the list is long or scanning would slow the user down. All internal copy is customized through translations: Optional, search, clear, loading, no-results heading and support copy, no-options copy, the create action label, and selected-count text. The "No results" heading and no-options fallback stay automatic unless overridden there. Use selection="multiple" when users can choose more than one option. Use creatable only when adding a missing option is a real next step; keep the create action pinned as the footer and let the parent open the creation dialog. For server-filtered or paged lists, use filterMode="manual" with queryChange, hasMore, loadingMore, and loadMore. If users need to compare a small set side by side, radios or a button group may be better.
guidance.cx-secret-display:
Use secret display for sensitive values that must be revealed, copied, or inspected with care. The default state should protect the value.

Make reveal and copy actions deliberate. Do not expose secrets just because there is enough space.
guidance.cx-search-field:
Use a search field when the user is narrowing a collection by typing. It should be easy to find, quick to clear, and forgiving of partial input.

Do not use placeholders. Use a visible label, ariaLabel, or nearby context to name what is being searched. Pair search with good empty states. A no-results state should help the user adjust, not leave them stuck.
guidance.cx-popover:
Use a popover for small supporting content or controls that belong to a trigger. It should be quick to open and quick to leave.

Sizing follows one contract: the content decides the width, the trigger sets the floor, and the viewport sets the ceiling. By default the surface grows to fit its content up to a compact cap so it reads as a local overlay, not a panel. Anchored surfaces pass minWidth so the popover never reads narrower than its trigger, and maxWidth when their content earns a wider cap. Reserve width for genuinely fixed layouts such as calendars. Popover content always sits in at least one soft island. Use multiple islands to create menu dividers instead of drawing divider lines. The surface itself carries no mood; tone comes from the content inside, such as a danger option row. Do not put long workflows in a popover. If the user needs to think, compare, or save work, use a larger surface.
guidance.cx-severity-tag:
Use a severity tag to show how serious something is. It helps users spot risk, urgency, or impact quickly.

Use severity sparingly and consistently. If everything is severe, nothing is.
guidance.cx-shortcut-key:
Use shortcut keys to show keyboard commands in a compact, recognizable way. They are helpful near menus, toolbars, and command references.

Only show shortcuts that actually work in that context. Wrong shortcut hints erode trust fast.
guidance.cx-slider:
Use a slider when the user is choosing a value by feel within a known range. It works best for approximate settings such as intensity, size, or volume.

Do not use a slider when the exact number matters. Give the user a number field or another exact control instead.
guidance.cx-snippet:
Use a snippet for short copyable text such as tokens, paths, commands, or IDs. It should make copying easier without turning the page into a code block.

Keep the snippet compact and readable. If the content wraps heavily, use a code block instead.
guidance.cx-spinner:
Use a spinner for very small loading states where preserving layout is not important. It should signal that a single control or small area is busy.

Avoid using spinners as the main page state. Larger waits need clearer feedback.
guidance.cx-split:
Use split layout when two areas need to sit beside each other with a clear relationship. It is useful for master-detail, summary-detail, and preview-edit patterns.

Keep the relationship obvious. If the two sides are unrelated, use separate sections instead.
guidance.cx-stack:
Use stack layout when content should flow vertically with consistent rhythm. It is the default layout choice for forms, settings, and grouped content.

Let the stack carry spacing instead of adding one-off margins. This keeps pages easier to maintain.
guidance.cx-sso-button:
Use an SSO button for signing in with a trusted provider. The provider name should be clear and the button should not look like a generic action.

Only show providers that are actually available. Authentication choices should feel reliable, not experimental.
guidance.cx-status-tag:
Use a status tag to show the current state of an item or process. It should help users scan lists and understand what needs attention.

Keep statuses stable and plain. Avoid clever labels that make state harder to interpret.
guidance.cx-switch:
Use a switch for a setting that takes effect as on or off. It is best for preferences, visibility, and feature toggles.

Use a checkbox instead when the choice is part of a form submission or the user is selecting items from a list.
guidance.cx-table:
Use a table when users need to compare rows and columns. It should make scanning, sorting, and finding patterns easier than cards or freeform layout would.

Put the most important columns first and keep cell content concise. Controls inside an active row remain independent, and opening a row context menu never activates or highlights that row. Column reorder and resize must offer the same outcome from pointer and keyboard, including pinned boundaries and cancellation. Use categorical severity for named levels and numeric score only for the 0–10 severity scale; preserve other scales and units as truthful text. If the row needs a story, it probably is not a table row.
guidance.cx-tabs:
Use tabs to switch between sibling views at the same level. Tabs should keep the user in place while changing the content below.

Keep labels short and stable. If there are too many tabs to scan, use overflow behavior rather than squeezing every label into view.
guidance.cx-tag:
Use a tag for compact metadata, categories, or applied filters. It should add context without becoming the main content. A dismissible tag keeps its trailing action visible and in the normal text flow so touch users can remove it on the first tap and long labels never sit underneath it.

Do not use tags as decorations. Each tag should help the user understand or act.
guidance.cx-tag-field:
Use tag field when the user needs to search, create, and manage multiple short values in one text-field surface. Selected tags stay inline with the live input; typing filters available tags, Up and Down move through suggestions, Enter toggles the active tag, and Space does the same when the query is empty. Escape closes the suggestions without discarding the query. With an empty input, Left or Backspace moves to the last selected tag; Backspace or Delete then removes it.

Keep Create as the final popover option. Mod+Enter opens it directly, a typed query prefills the tag name, Cancel returns to the same query, and a created tag is selected immediately. Use a Select [thing] placeholder such as Select tags or Select recipients. Do not use tag field for a single choice or for long free-form content.
guidance.cx-steps:
Use steps when a process has a known sequence. Pass the exact sequence being presented and address the current position in that same array; derive conditional steps before they reach the component. The indicator is passive and is never disabled.

Do not use steps for loose navigation. The order should matter. labelMode only changes what is visible: every step name and its current, completed, upcoming, or needs-attention status remains available to assistive technology.
guidance.cx-textarea:
Use a textarea for longer free text such as notes, descriptions, and comments. It gives the user room to think and revise.

Do not use placeholders. Put prompts, examples, and constraints in hint text. The visible hint or validation message must remain associated with the native textarea; validation replaces the hint, and only an error marks the field invalid. Do not use it for short values that should stay scannable in a form. A text field is cleaner for those.
guidance.cx-time-field:
Use time field when the user needs a specific time. Each hour or minute segment behaves as one editable unit: typing replaces that segment, complete values advance naturally, and one-digit values zero-pad when committed. Users can move with Tab, Left, Right, or a colon; adjust with Up and Down; and paste familiar forms such as 9, 930, 13:00, or 9:30 PM.

Use minuteStep for a real minute grid and min or max for allowed bounds. Impossible or out-of-range values stay visible with local recovery instead of silently changing or disappearing. Pair the field with a date when the day matters, and add a hint only when format or limits are not already clear from context.
guidance.cx-toast:
Use a toast for short feedback after an action. It should confirm, warn, or explain something lightweight without interrupting the user. Plain non-dismissible information may close after five seconds and must pause its remaining lifetime while hovered or focused.

Any visible action makes the toast persistent and dismissible; actionable notifications never auto-dismiss, and pressing an action does not close them implicitly. Explicitly dismissible toasts also persist. Do not use toasts for critical information or anything the user must read later. Important messages need a persistent place.
guidance.cx-toggle-button:
Use a toggle button for an action that can stay on or off, especially in toolbars. Off uses a quiet button surface; on uses a raised emphasis surface, so the pressed state remains obvious in every theme. Keep its accessible name stable when the icon changes with state.

Provide text or a base icon. Do not use it for navigation. If the user is switching views, tabs are clearer.
guidance.cx-toggle-chip:
Use a toggle chip for compact filter choices that can be turned on or off. It works well when several chips can sit together.

Keep chip labels short. If the choice needs explanation, use a larger control.
guidance.cx-toggle-chip-group:
Use a toggle chip group for a set of compact filters or modes. It should help users scan available choices and see what is active.

Do not use it for high-stakes choices. Chips are lightweight by nature.
guidance.cx-tooltip:
Use a tooltip for short help that explains an icon, label, or small control. It should clarify something the user is already near.

Do not hide essential information in a tooltip. Tooltips are support, not the main interface.
guidance.cx-tree-view:
Use a tree view for nested structures where the user needs to expand, collapse, and understand hierarchy. It is useful for folders, scopes, and grouped navigation.

Keep the tree readable. If the hierarchy is too deep, add search or a simpler way to jump.
guidance.cx-trend-tag:
Use a trend tag to show direction or change in a compact way. It works best beside a metric or list item where the comparison matters.

Make the baseline clear. A trend without context can look meaningful while saying very little.
guidance.cx-wizard-dialog:
Use a wizard dialog for a genuinely sequential task whose later decisions depend on earlier ones. Pass the exact step sequence currently presented and keep index in that sequence. When a choice changes the branch, the owner derives the new array and explicitly remaps the current step by id; the dialog never searches hidden steps or chooses a replacement.

Let Back preserve compatible work, make the final outcome explicit, and keep every visually suppressed step label available as an accessible name.
